production_notes: [VERIFY] Music licensing terms of royalty-free libraries, editor music libraries and AI music tools must be checked against current official terms. The voiceover teaches licence checking as a principle and names no licence, library or tool terms as settled. Lucas's track and its licence are hypothetical.
[VERIFY] content.md's guidance on music level relative to voice is a general starting point. The voiceover gives no decibel numbers; it says 'well below the voice' and 'adjust by ear'.

[VERSION] Editor features (automatic music lowering under speech, noise reduction, safe-area guides), common export settings and platform requirements must be checked against the live tools. The voiceover says 'if your editor has one' and 'check each platform's current guidance'.
[REGION] CapCut availability differs by country; learners may use the fallback editor from Lesson 11.
This lesson is not a screen demo: the worked example uses slides and stock footage only.
Lucas and the surf school in Florianópolis are hypothetical; stock footage must show no real surf school name, brand or logo. Music under this video must itself be licensed for the course.

Hook.voiceover: Viewers often forgive a small visual problem. They rarely forgive a voice they cannot hear. Sound is half of your video, and the export is the version people actually watch. This is capstone step two.

Explain.voiceover: In the last lesson, you built your rough cut. Now you make it sound right, and export it for the places people will watch it.

slide.title: Sound, Music and Export Settings
slide.body: AI Video Production and Motion · Lesson 12 of 14

Explain.voiceover: Most short videos have three layers of sound. The voice, from your narration or avatar, is the most important. Music sets the mood and the pace. And sound effects, like a door, waves or a coffee pour, make generated clips feel real.

slide.title: Three layers of sound
slide.body: Three stacked tracks: Voice (most important, largest) · Music (mood and pace) · Sound effects (door, waves, coffee pour).

Explain.voiceover: The voice must always be clear. So set the voice first, loud and clear without distortion. Then bring the music in well below it, and adjust by ear. If your editor can lower music automatically under speech, use it.

slide.title: Balancing levels
slide.body: 1. Voice first: loud, clear, no distortion · 2. Music well below the voice, adjust by ear · 3. Automatic lowering under speech, if your editor has it

Explain.voiceover: Then listen twice, on phone speakers and on headphones. A mix that sounds good on headphones can sound unclear on a phone.
Explain.stock_query: person listening to phone speaker closely

Explain.voiceover: Now music. Only use music whose licence allows your use. Royalty-free does not always mean free for any use. Ask three questions. Can you use it commercially? On which platforms? Do you need to credit the creator?

slide.title: Check the music licence
slide.body: Commercial use allowed? · Which platforms? · Credit required? Note: royalty-free does not always mean free for any use.

Explain.voiceover: Editors, stock libraries and AI music tools each have their own terms, and they change. Save a copy of the licence with your project. And never use a popular song just because you own a copy of it.
Explain.on_screen_text: Save the licence with your project

Explain.voiceover: Next, export. Plan two versions. A horizontal version, sixteen by nine, for websites and presentations. And a vertical version, nine by sixteen, for short-form social apps. Platform requirements change, so check each platform's current guidance.

slide.title: Two versions
slide.body: Left: 16:9 horizontal frame, websites and presentations. Right: 9:16 vertical frame, short-form social apps. Note: check each platform's current guidance.

Explain.voiceover: On vertical apps, buttons and text cover parts of the screen, especially the bottom and the right side. So keep captions and important details inside the central safe area.

slide.title: The safe area
slide.body: Vertical phone frame with grey blocks at the bottom and right edge for app buttons. A dashed teal box in the centre labelled safe area, with captions inside it.

Explain.voiceover: Mixing sound is like a dinner conversation in a restaurant. The music is the background noise of the room. If it becomes too loud, nobody at the table can hear the person speaking, however interesting they are.
Explain.on_screen_text: Music is the room, not the speaker

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's see an example. Lucas runs a surf school in Florianópolis, Brazil. The school is made up for this lesson. His eighty-second video is edited. Now he works on sound and export.
Demonstrate.stock_query: surf lesson for beginners on sunny beach

Demonstrate.voiceover: First, he makes the voice clear and steady, and removes a short hum with noise reduction. Then he chooses a calm acoustic track. He reads the licence. For his track, commercial use is allowed and credit is optional. He saves a copy in his project folder.

slide.title: Voice and music
slide.body: 1. Voice clear and steady; hum removed · 2. Calm acoustic track · 3. Licence read: commercial use allowed, credit optional · 4. Copy saved in the project folder

Demonstrate.voiceover: He places the music under the whole video, well below the voice. He raises it slightly only in the four-second opening, where there is no narration. He adds two sound effects. Waves on the beach shot, and a board hitting the water.

slide.title: Lucas's mix
slide.body: Timeline: voice track across the video; music track low throughout, slightly higher in the first 4 seconds; two small sound-effect blocks labelled waves and board on water.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Then he listens on his phone. The music hides the word beginners. So he lowers the music further, until every word is clear.
Demonstrate.stock_query: man listening to video on smartphone at beach

Demonstrate.voiceover: He exports a sixteen by nine version at ten eighty p. Then he duplicates the project, changes it to nine by sixteen, and reframes each clip, so the surfer stays in the centre. He moves the captions up into the safe area, and exports the vertical version.

slide.title: Horizontal, then vertical
slide.body: Left: 16:9 frame of a surfer, 1080p, exported. Right: 9:16 frame, reframed so the surfer is centred, captions moved up into the safe area.

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is loud music that sounds exciting on headphones, but hides the voice on a phone. Another is changing the aspect ratio without reframing, so subjects are cut off and captions sit under app buttons.

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, the voice comes first. Music and sound effects sit clearly below it, and you test the mix on phone speakers. Second, use only music whose licence allows your use, and save a copy of the licence. Third, export a horizontal and a vertical version, reframe each shot, and keep captions inside the safe area.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Voice first; test on a phone. 2. Check and save the music licence. 3. 16:9 and 9:16, reframed, captions in the safe area.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn, with capstone step two. Add music and one to three sound effects, balance the levels on a phone and on headphones, and save the music licence. Then export one horizontal and one vertical version. It takes about thirty-five minutes. Next lesson: Publishing Responsibly, Disclosure, Consent and Rights.
